doc.title: Iola Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, CT, July 17, 2011

title: Monterey concert version and renewed interest
summary: The show never reached Broadway; Jimmy Lyons had them do a concert version at Monterey, and there is new interest in it as a period piece.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: That’s wonderful. And probably mounting this co-production, trying to get it on Broadway, I can’t imagine the hoops that you’d have to.

Well it never came about. Jimmy Lyons at the Monterey Jazz Festival telephoned us. We had moved to Connecticut by that time, and said “I want you do to it in Monterey.” Well of course it’s not a situation where you can mount a musical in Monterey. And so I decided okay, we’ll do it as a concert version with narration of most of the songs. So we had Louis Armstrong and his band, and Paul wasn’t in it but Dave and Joe and Eugene. And Lambert, Hendricks and Bavan, Annie had left by that time. And it was a super hit at the Monterey Jazz Festival, and especially among the musicians. I remember Dizzy coming backstage afterwards, really with tears in his eyes. And he said, “I couldn’t believe my ears.”
Wow. And to put it on in an outdoor venue like that I mean — to go across — that’s great.
It’s interesting, in more recent times there’s been a renewed interest in it. Somebody from England has inquired about it and of course the economic times are bad over there. He

had applied for a grant which he didn’t get, but is still holding out hope of maybe doing something. And there’ve been other people who have shown interest in it, not as a full- blown stage production but maybe a concert production similar to what we had done in Monterey. They are saying enough time has gone by now that it is sort of a reflection of that period in our history.
So you think it could almost stand as it is, as opposed to trying to update it?

I think it’s better to be a period piece actually, to reflect the thinking of, well, 1960. The Civil Rights Bill hadn’t been signed yet. There was still segregation. We’ve come a long ways since then.
